candidates.attacker_control: The runtime value supplied by the application to a @Path-annotated service-method parameter (e.g. a user name, id, or filename taken from untrusted input). The library itself cannot know the value's origin; it performs the substitution and URL construction with no dot-segment validation or warning.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified there is exactly one substitution site (search for 'relativeUrl.replace' returns only RequestBuilder.java:94) and one caller (ParameterHandler.java:99). Checked the encoding logic: with encoded=false the characters '/' and '%' are percent-encoded (lines 103/127), so a raw multi-segment '../..' payload cannot cross segments; the default-mode exploit is limited to a bare '.'/'..' value removing one segment. OkHttp does not reject dot segments, it normalizes them, so it does not mitigate the escape. The @Path Javadoc (http/Path.java:40-49) documents encoded=true only as 'already URL encoded' and gives no traversal warning. Searches for 'traversal' / 'PATH_TRAVERSAL' return no matches, i.e. no mitigation exists in the snapshot. No tests are included to check intended behavior, and the code was not executed.
candidates.impact: Attacker-influenced outbound requests leave the intended base-path prefix on the same origin and can reach sibling endpoints such as /admin, /internal, or other API versions that the call site was not supposed to address, defeating path-prefix-based routing or authorization assumptions and expanding the reachable server surface (an SSRF-like request-forgery primitive within the target origin). Dot-segment traversal alone cannot change scheme/host, so this is not arbitrary-host SSRF.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The interface method's relative URL contains a {name} placeholder inside a path segment with a matching @Path parameter. 2) The application passes attacker-influenced data as that parameter. 3) For multi-level traversal, the annotation must use encoded=true (a documented supported mode) so '/' and '%' are left intact; with default encoding only a bare '.'/'..' value can shift one segment. 4) The base URL has a path prefix that the target server treats as a routing/authorization boundary.
candidates.root_cause: RequestBuilder.addPathParam (lines 89-95) replaces the "{name}" placeholder with canonicalizeForPath(value, encoded) and never rejects '.'/'..' (or percent-encoded '%2e') path segments. canonicalizeForPath deliberately leaves '/', '%' and '.' untouched when alreadyEncoded is true (line 103 and mirrored line 127; '.' is not in PATH_SEGMENT_ALWAYS_ENCODE_SET at line 33), so values such as "../admin" or "%2e%2e/admin" survive substitution. The substituted relative URL is then resolved against baseUrl via HttpUrl (baseUrl.resolve at line 197, or baseUrl.newBuilder at line 149), and OkHttp's canonicalization resolves '.'/'..'/'%2e' segments by popping path segments, producing a request path outside the intended base prefix. A single-segment escape also exists with default encoding because '.' is never percent-encoded, so a bare ".." value removes the preceding path segment.
candidates.title: Path traversal via unsanitized @Path parameter substitution in RequestBuilder.addPathParam
candidates.trace: ServiceMethod.Builder.parseParameterAnnotation builds ParameterHandler.Path with path.encoded() (ServiceMethod.java:405) -> ParameterHandler.Path.apply calls builder.addPathParam(name, value, encoded) (ParameterHandler.java:99) -> RequestBuilder.addPathParam does relativeUrl.replace("{"+name+"}", canonicalizeForPath(value, encoded)) with no dot-segment check (RequestBuilder.java:94) -> with encoded=true, canonicalizeForPath copies '/', '%' and '.' verbatim (RequestBuilder.java:103, 127, 139-141) -> RequestBuilder.build (or addQueryParam) resolves the substituted relative URL against baseUrl (RequestBuilder.java:197 / 149) -> OkHttp HttpUrl normalization resolves '.'/'..'/'%2e' segments by popping them. Example shape: base https://api.example.com/v1/ with @GET("users/{id}") and id="../admin" yields https://api.example.com/admin (no runtime execution performed; based on source semantics of OkHttp HttpUrl.resolve used at the call site).
candidates.unverified: Runtime behavior was not executed and no tests exist in the snapshot; the reachable traversal depth depends on OkHttp 3.10.0's dot-segment handling of raw '..' versus '%2e' variants. Whether a concrete deployment feeds untrusted data into such a @Path parameter is application-dependent and cannot be determined from library sources alone. The exact server-side impact depends on how the target maps paths.
candidates.weakness_type: Path traversal / improper neutralization of dot-segments in URL path (CWE-22-like)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned 182-file source snapshot (get_source_scope reported no sensitive-name/path, symlink, or size exclusions; only binary-like files are skipped by tooling). Core library files were read in full or substantially: RequestBuilder, ParameterHandler, ServiceMethod, Utils, OkHttpCall, Platform, Response, Converter, Call, CallAdapter, DefaultCallAdapterFactory, ExecutorCallAdapterFactory, BuiltInConverters, HttpException, and the http annotations. Adapters (rxjava/rxjava2 slots read around cancellation/error delivery), converters (Gson/Moshi/SimpleXML/Scalars response paths), retrofit-mock (NetworkBehavior, BehaviorCall, Calls) and the samples were skimmed and searched. Notable coverage gaps: no test sources, and retrofit/src/main/java/retrofit2/Retrofit.java is absent although referenced by ServiceMethod/Converter/CallAdapter, so builder-side validation (baseUrl/create) could not be inspected. Static website assets were not security-relevant.
limitations: No tests in the snapshot; behavior could not be validated against expected unit-test semantics.
Retrofit.java is missing from the snapshot even though it is referenced by other sources, so create()/Builder validation logic is uninspected and the module would not compile as included.
No execution, compilation, or runtime probing was performed (read-only review); the traversal is inferred from source semantics of OkHttp HttpUrl.resolve.
Many adapter/converter files were only skimmed or search-inspected, not read line by line; a subtle issue there cannot be fully excluded.

The snapshot's commit history/patch state is unavailable, so whether the missing dot-segment check is a deliberately reverted fix versus the historical vulnerable state cannot be determined from the tree alone.

rejected_leads.lead: @Url parameter accepts arbitrary absolute URLs (SSRF-shaped behavior)
rejected_leads.reason: Documented API semantics: @Url is meant to be the full URL supplied by the caller; the library intentionally performs no allow-listing. No source evidence of a library-level trust-boundary violation beyond intended use.

rejected_leads.lead: encoded=true call sites can cause a protocol-relative value to change the request host (e.g. whole-path placeholder with value '//evil.com/')
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible adjacent behavior but a distinct root cause, requires the unusual whole-placeholder URL plus encoded=true, and could not be verified against OkHttp 3.10.0 semantics from this snapshot; left unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: Full buffering of error response bodies in OkHttpCall.parseResponse/Utils.buffer allows memory pressure from a hostile server
rejected_leads.reason: Upstream intended behavior; impact is bounded by the response the server sends and the client's own read path, with no evidence of unbounded amplification or missing validation.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflective trusted MethodHandles.Lookup construction in Platform.Java8.invokeDefaultMethod
rejected_leads.reason: Standard upstream implementation for calling interface default methods; inputs are library-internal (service interface metadata), not attacker-controlled.

rejected_leads.lead: @Header/@HeaderMap/@Part names and values could inject headers
rejected_leads.reason: OkHttp Headers.Builder rejects CR/LF in names and values, and these values originate from application code, not the remote peer; no evidence of a reachable injection in this snapshot.

summary: Snapshot is Retrofit 2.4.1-SNAPSHOT (182 source files; tests and the central Retrofit.java are not present). The strongest source-evidenced issue is that @Path parameter values are substituted into the method's relative URL without any rejection of dot-segments, so an attacker-influenced path value can escape the intended base-URL path prefix when OkHttp normalizes the resulting URL. This matches the known Retrofit path-traversal weakness (RequestBuilder.addPathParam); a dot-segment check (e.g. rejecting '.'/'..'/%2e) is absent everywhere in the snapshot. Other inspected areas (adapters, converters, mock module, samples, platform/reflection code) showed no stronger candidate.
